faq.a: No. HDV requires HBsAg for entry and assembly; without HBV infection it cannot replicate.
faq.q: Can hepatitis D occur without hepatitis B?

faq.a: HDV induces a stronger cytopathic immune response, leading to higher liver enzyme elevations and faster fibrosis.
faq.q: Why is HDV infection more severe than HBV alone?

faq.a: There is no direct vaccine; preventing HBV with the hepatitis B vaccine also prevents HDV.
faq.q: Is there a vaccine for hepatitis D?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with known chronic HBV presents with sudden jaundice and INR 2.0 – what is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Consider HDV superinfection; order anti‑HDV IgM and start supportive care while arranging interferon if resources allow.

In a child with acute liver failure, HBsAg is positive but anti‑HBc IgM is negative – which additional test clarifies the cause? — Test anti‑HDV IgM; a positive result indicates HDV coinfection causing fulminant hepatitis.
Why does hepatitis B vaccination protect against hepatitis D? — HBV vaccine induces anti‑HBsAg antibodies, removing the envelope protein HDV needs to form infectious particles.
A patient on tenofovir for HBV develops worsening ALT and bilirubin – what should you suspect? — Possible HDV superinfection; check anti‑HDV IgM/IgG and HDV RNA.

What is the rationale for using pegylated interferon‑α in HDV infection? — It directly inhibits HDV replication; however, it is costly and has many side effects, limiting use in low‑resource settings.

How would you differentiate HDV superinfection from an HBV flare clinically and with labs? — Superinfection shows higher bilirubin, INR, and anti‑HDV IgM positivity, whereas a flare shows only HBV markers rising.
A pregnant woman is HBsAg‑positive; should you screen for HDV? — Yes, because HDV can cause severe disease in the mother and increase perinatal transmission risk.
What are the key public‑health measures to prevent HDV in East Africa? — Universal HBV vaccination, safe injection practices, screening blood donors, and education on sexual transmission.
ai.title: Hepatitis D (Delta Hepatitis)
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: HDV is a defective RNA virus that needs hepatitis B surface antigen to replicate. It causes more severe acute hepatitis and accelerates chronic liver disease, especially in low‑resource settings where HBV is common.

b: Defective virus – requires HBV for entry and assembly
Transmitted via blood, sexual contact, perinatal, and unsafe injections
sections.p: Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a small, circular, single‑stranded RNA virus that cannot produce its own envelope. It hijacks the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) to form infectious particles, so infection occurs only as HBV coinfection or superinfection.

b: Circular RNA ~1.7 kb, high mutation rate
Only two antigens: small (S‑HDAg) and large (L‑HDAg)
sections.p: HDV belongs to the Deltavirus genus. Its genome encodes only two proteins: the delta antigen (HDAg) and a ribozyme that assists replication. The virus replicates in the nucleus using host RNA polymerase II.

b: Coinfection: simultaneous exposure to HBV and HDV
Superinfection: HDV infection of a chronic HBV carrier
sections.p: Because HDV needs HBsAg, it follows the same routes as hepatitis B. In endemic East African settings, unsafe needle reuse, traditional scarification, and mother‑to‑child transmission are common.

b: Acute severe hepatitis – higher ALT, bilirubin, INR
Chronic superinfection – rapid fibrosis, earlier cirrhosis
Higher mortality in fulminant liver failure, especially children
sections.p: HDV infection produces an acute hepatitis that is often more severe than HBV alone, with higher rates of jaundice, hepatic necrosis, and fulminant liver failure. In chronic HBV carriers, superinfection accelerates cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Serology and nucleic‑acid testing identify HDV. In low‑resource hospitals, the most available tests are anti‑HDV IgM/IgG and HDV RNA PCR when possible.

t.b: Is this a recent infection? Positive IgM indicates acute or recent superinfection.
Has the patient been exposed? Persistent IgG suggests chronic infection.
Is the virus actively replicating? Detects viral load; not always available – if absent, rely on serology plus high ALT/ bilirubin in HBV‑positive patient.
Is HBV present to act as a helper? Required for any HDV diagnosis.

b: Suppress HBV with tenofovir or entecavir – reduces new HDV particles
Peg‑IFN‑α for 48 weeks in selected patients – modest SVR, monitor for depression
Vaccinate against HBV – prevents HDV infection entirely
sections.p: No HDV‑specific therapy is widely available in low‑resource settings. The main goal is to suppress HBV replication, which indirectly limits HDV. Pegylated interferon‑α is the only proven agent but is costly and has significant side effects.

t.b: If unavailable, use bedside assessment of jaundice, encephalopathy, and ascites.
Is there cirrhosis or portal hypertension? Guides prognosis and need for referral.

b: Always test for HDV in any HBsAg‑positive patient with severe acute hepatitis or rapid fibrosis.
Remember that HDV cannot exist without HBsAg – HBV vaccination eliminates HDV risk.
In fulminant cases, early referral for liver transplant is critical; supportive care includes vitamin K, lactulose, and monitoring INR.
sections.p: Focus on the dependency of HDV on HBV, the clinical picture of a more aggressive hepatitis, and the limited therapeutic options.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly rising bilirubin >10 mg/dL with INR >1.5
Encephalopathy (any grade) in a hepatitis D patient
Signs of decompensated cirrhosis: ascites, variceal bleed, hepatic encephalopathy
